sourceTitle: Watching the Sky, Interpreting the Odds
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: EN/C1 independently authored Asteroids test: uncertainty, evidence and planetary-defence reasoning. Human content review pending.

tabs.title: Interpreting the evidence
tabs.description: Read between the lines and establish the main argument.

tabs.title: Evidence in practice
tabs.description: Transfer scientific reasoning to new situations.

questions.q: What epistemic distinction does the writer draw when discussing an asteroid's trajectory?
choices: The asteroid's physical motion cannot be predicted even in principle.
Uncertainty is mainly in our knowledge of its path, not in whether physical laws apply.
Astronomers disagree about whether asteroids orbit the Sun.
The uncertainty exists only when reporters use imprecise headlines.
questions.explanation: The author distinguishes a lawful physical orbit from an incompletely observed trajectory.

questions.q: How should readers interpret an increase in an estimated collision probability during early tracking?
choices: It is proof that the asteroid has suddenly changed speed.
It means the risk is statistically certain until scientists deny it.
It reveals that the first measurements were intentionally inaccurate.
It may be part of narrowing a range of trajectories, not a simple worsening of the situation.
questions.explanation: An apparently higher risk can arise while successive measurements constrain possible orbits.

questions.q: What is the deeper engineering problem raised beyond hitting an asteroid?
choices: Choosing a sufficiently dramatic spacecraft design to reassure the public.
Deciding which government should publicly announce the mission first.
Predicting the physical effect and checking whether the intended orbital change occurred.
Proving that all possible impact scenarios are equally manageable.
questions.explanation: The text identifies target understanding and follow-up measurement as essential engineering capabilities.

questions.q: Why is the debris plume after DART's impact an especially important observation?
choices: It indicates that the deflection depended on more than the spacecraft's direct momentum.
It proves Dimorphos must have been a solid, uniform boulder.
It suggests the mission's observed orbital change was an optical illusion.
It makes further study of the system unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The ejecta amplified the impact's effect, showing why material properties matter.

questions.q: Why does the writer contrast scientific descriptions with alarmist headlines?
choices: To make the case that journalism should never cover asteroid science.
To show how accurate uncertainty communication differs from unsupported certainty.
To demonstrate that researchers and journalists use incompatible measurements.
To suggest public safety is irrelevant to curiosity-driven space research.
questions.explanation: The author presents accurate risk language as intellectual honesty, against compressed warnings.

questions.q: Why does the author emphasise that DART produced a result rather than a guarantee?
choices: The spacecraft's collision was impossible to observe independently.
The target asteroid had not been identified before the mission.
The result is conditional on physical structure and available time to act.
The experiment showed that momentum transfer does not change orbits.
questions.explanation: A particular demonstration cannot guarantee success under different structures, deflection directions and warning times.

questions.q: Which pair of communication failures is the writer attempting to avoid?
choices: Providing too many observations and coordinating too closely.
Warning about distant objects and publishing detailed measurements.
Treating all probability estimates as exactly equivalent.
Overstating the urgency of every approach and dismissing small risks altogether.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph warns against both indiscriminate alarm and complacent dismissal.

questions.q: An early impact estimate rises, but the range of possible trajectories is shrinking. Which explanation is best?
choices: The asteroid must be changing course because of unseen forces.
The new measurements refine a provisional model, which may temporarily raise the estimated risk.
The previous telescope images should be discarded as useless.
The higher number itself confirms a future collision.
questions.explanation: The text explains that narrowing uncertainty may produce temporary increases before resolution.

questions.q: A planner proposes deflecting a poorly understood rubble pile without studying its structure. What question is missing?
choices: How its material properties could influence the momentum transfer and resulting orbit.
Whether a sufficiently large explosion would be more impressive in public footage.
Why scientists should continue observing a target after the mission.
Whether its name is familiar to the public.
questions.explanation: The Dimorphos findings show that material properties significantly determine deflection outcomes.

questions.q: What is the strongest reason to fund asteroid surveys even without an identified immediate threat?
choices: They guarantee that a collision with Earth will never occur.
They remove the need to build instruments for future missions.
They make possible impacts more exciting subjects for science communication.
Early knowledge and international coordination make later proportionate intervention possible.
questions.explanation: The conclusion identifies surveys and data sharing as necessary conditions for effective decisions.
